title: Market Risk, Lesson 9: Mapping positions onto risk factors
subtitle: Nobody models every single bond - and how you choose to aggregate decides the VaR number
whyItMatters: Before VaR can be computed, thousands of positions have to be reduced to a manageable set of risk factors. This step is rarely discussed but influences the result more than most of the technical choices that follow it, because any risk aggregated away during mapping never reappears in the output.
openingQuestion: Why is VaR not computed directly on each individual instrument in the portfolio?
openingOptions: Because the covariance matrix grows with the square of the instrument count
Because regulators require aggregation into standardised factor groups
Because a single instrument has too little volatility for VaR to be computed
Because VaR is only defined at portfolio level, not at instrument level
explanation: With n instruments, the covariance matrix needs about n(n+1)/2 parameters. A thousand bonds is more than half a million parameters, and most of the pairs have too little common trading history to be estimated reliably. Mapping reduces the instruments onto a far smaller factor set - a few dozen points on the curve, a few equity indices, a few currency pairs - small enough to estimate robustly while keeping the risk that matters.

diagram.label: Thousands of individual positions in the portfolio
Mapped onto a shared, far smaller set of risk factors
Covariance matrix estimated on that factor set
Specific risk lost in aggregation must be handled separately, not ignored

realWorldExample.company: Cash flow mapping of a bond portfolio
realWorldExample.description: The standard approach splits each bond into its cash flows and allocates each one across the two nearest grid points on the curve, holding present value constant and holding market risk constant. A seven-year bond therefore becomes part of the five-year point and part of the ten-year point - and every analysis downstream sees it exactly that way.

quiz.question: What is the governing principle when allocating a cash flow across two neighbouring grid points?
options: Put the whole cash flow on the nearer of the two grid points
Split the value equally between the two closest curve points
Preserve present value and preserve market risk exposure
Allocate by the relative liquidity of the two grid points
quiz.explanation: A mapping is only valid if it neither creates nor destroys value and does not change the amount of risk being carried. Splitting evenly, or dumping everything on the nearer point, each violate at least one of those two conditions, and that error runs straight through into the final VaR number. Liquidity is a good reason to prefer certain maturities when choosing the grid in the first place, but it is not a rule for distributing a cash flow once the grid exists.

quiz.question: Scenario: a portfolio holds 1,000 instruments. Roughly how many parameters does the full covariance matrix need?
options: About 1,000,000 (= 1,000², both matrix halves)
Exactly 1,000, one variance parameter per instrument
About 2,000, a variance and a mean for each instrument
quiz.explanation: The matrix is symmetric, so only the upper triangle plus the diagonal is needed: n(n+1)/2 = 1,000 × 1,001 ÷ 2 ≈ 500,500. Counting the full square double-counts every pair. That figure is why mapping is not a convenience for tidiness but the condition under which the estimation problem has a solution at all, given that a few hundred days of history cannot support half a million parameters.

quiz.question: Which risk is lost when a corporate bond is mapped onto the government curve?
options: The credit spread risk specific to that issuer
Interest rate risk at the long end of the curve
Reinvestment risk on the future coupon payments
Liquidity risk across the entire bond market
quiz.explanation: Mapping onto the government curve keeps the interest rate risk and throws away the spread - precisely the component that moves most violently in a crisis. Duration exposure at the long end survives the mapping, because that is what the curve points are there to represent. Reinvestment risk concerns the coupons rather than the discount factors, and market-wide liquidity risk is not a factor the curve carries either. The fix is to add spread factors by rating band and sector, not to ignore the gap.

quiz.question: Why does coarser mapping tend to understate VaR?
options: Because a smaller factor set always has lower volatility
Because collapsing to one factor implicitly assumes perfect correlation
Because the mapping step always lowers the portfolio's present value
Because the history of an aggregate factor is usually shorter
quiz.explanation: When two different positions are collapsed onto the same factor, the model treats them as moving identically - so the idiosyncratic component that makes them diverge disappears, and offsetting positions look like a perfect hedge. That is why the specific risk lost in aggregation has to be added back explicitly. A smaller factor set is not inherently less volatile, a valid mapping is built to preserve present value, and the length of the factor history is a separate estimation problem.

quiz.question: What is the core trade-off in choosing how many risk factors to use?
options: Fewer factors raise VaR but make it easier to explain upward
More factors are always more accurate but take longer to compute
More factors retain more risk but estimate less robustly
Factor count changes nothing but the speed of the calculation
quiz.explanation: Adding factors means retaining more risk detail, but it also means estimating more parameters from the same amount of data - and estimation noise can do more damage than the detail just preserved. This is the bias-variance trade-off familiar from every modelling problem. Coarser mapping pushes VaR down rather than up, extra factors buy accuracy only where the data supports them, and the choice is a risk decision rather than a question of computing time.

practicePrompt.question: A corporate bond portfolio is mapped entirely onto the government yield curve. The VaR it produces is far below the loss actually taken in a stress episode. Why?
options: Credit spread was aggregated away and never added back explicitly
The government curve moves more than the corporate curve does
Too many risk factors made the covariance matrix unstable
Mapping onto the government curve always overstates VaR
practicePrompt.explanation: Mapping onto the government curve retains interest rate risk and discards credit spread risk - exactly the part that blows out under stress, when government yields can fall while spreads widen sharply. Coarser mapping pushes VaR downward, because collapsing many positions onto one factor implicitly assumes perfect correlation between them and cancels out the specific risk. The fix is not to abandon mapping - without it, 1,000 instruments would need roughly half a million covariance parameters - but to add the specific risk back explicitly.

keyTakeaways: Mapping is what makes the estimation feasible: n instruments need n(n+1)/2 covariance parameters
Cash flow allocation must preserve present value and preserve market risk exposure
Coarse mapping understates VaR, because it implicitly assumes positions on one factor are perfectly correlated
Specific risk lost in aggregation must be added back explicitly, never treated as gone

summary.keyIdea: Mapping decides the VaR number more than most of the technical choices that follow it, because any risk aggregated away here never shows up in the output.

application.message: When reviewing a VaR model, ask where the corporate bonds are mapped. If they land only on the government curve with no credit spread factor, the model is blind to exactly the component that moves most in a crisis.

sections.text: Before any VaR formula comes a step almost nobody discusses: reducing thousands of positions to a factor set small enough to estimate. The choices made here decide the final number more than the calculation method does.
Why individual instruments cannot be kept

A covariance matrix for n instruments needs about n(n+1)/2 parameters. A thousand instruments is more than half a million numbers to estimate, and most of the pairs have too little common trading history. The result would be a matrix full of noise, and no calculation downstream can repair noise at the input.
The two conditions of a valid mapping

Splitting a bond into cash flows and allocating them across neighbouring grid points is only correct if two things are held constant: present value and market risk exposure. Violating the first means creating or evaporating money; violating the second means changing the very thing you are trying to measure.
The risk that disappears during aggregation

When two different corporate bonds are both mapped onto one point on the government curve, the model treats them as the same thing. What made them different - their own credit spreads - vanishes, and that is exactly the component that moves most when markets tighten. It has to be brought back through a dedicated factor rather than treated as already handled.

sections.label: Worth remembering
sections.text: The coarser the mapping, the lower the VaR, because aggregation implicitly assumes perfect correlation and opposing positions appear to offset each other completely.

A covariance matrix for n instruments needs n(n+1)/2 parameters. With a thousand instruments that is 500,500 numbers to estimate - from a few hundred days of data. The resulting matrix is almost certain to be singular and stuffed with spurious correlations. Reduce to 20 risk factors and only 210 parameters remain, estimable from that same data set. Mapping is not a computational shortcut, it is the condition under which the problem has a solution.

sections.label: The two conditions of a valid split
sections.text: Splitting a seven-year bond across the five-year and ten-year grid points must hold two quantities constant: present value and interest rate sensitivity. If the bond has duration 6.5, the weight w on the five-year point solves 5w + 10(1 − w) = 6.5, giving w = 0.7 - that is, 70% of the value on the five-year point and 30% on the ten-year. Drop the second condition and split by present value alone, and VaR is already wrong at the first step, before any statistical formula has been applied.

The most important thing to remember is the direction of the error. Coarser mapping makes VaR LOWER, rather than wrong in either direction at random. When two different corporate bonds are collapsed onto one point of the government curve, the model implicitly assumes they move identically - so two opposing positions look like a complete offset, and the basis risk between them drops out of the number. That is why choosing the factor set is a risk decision rather than a technical one.
